The chain rule is the fundamental technique for differentiating composite functions. If y equals f of g of x, then the derivative with respect to x equals f prime of g of x times g prime of x—that is, the derivative of the outer function evaluated at the inner function, times the derivative of the inner function. You might hear it called "the derivative of the outside times the derivative of the inside." The chain rule is one of the most-applied rules in calculus and is essential for handling complex expressions like sine of x squared, e to the power of three x, or two x plus one all to the fifth power.

Consider a few common examples. The derivative of sine of x squared is cosine of x squared times two x, where the outer function is sine and the inner function is x squared. The derivative of e to the three x equals e to the three x times three, with the outer function being e to the u and the inner being three x. The derivative of two x plus one to the fifth power equals five times two x plus one to the fourth power, times two, which simplifies to ten times two x plus one to the fourth.

The chain rule applies to any depth of nesting. Take sine of cosine of x: its derivative is cosine of cosine of x times negative sine of x. Combined with the power rule, the chain rule tells us that the derivative of f of x to the n equals n times f of x to the n minus one, times f prime of x. When you use implicit differentiation—differentiating both sides of an equation where y is defined implicitly—you introduce chain-rule terms.

The chain rule is the third leg of differentiation, alongside the power rule and product rule. It is indispensable because most real-world functions are composite: you don't often differentiate sine of x or x squared in isolation, but rather sine of x squared or x squared plus one to the third power. Mastering the chain rule is what separates "can do calculus" from "understands calculus." It also appears in higher dimensions as the multivariable chain rule, expressed through Jacobian matrices in vector calculus. Quiz-bowl questions often test chain rule combined with other rules: differentiate x squared plus one to the third power times sine of x, and you need product rule, chain rule, and power rule working together.
